title: Methods
text:
Each indicator follows the same pipeline:

Download raw open data with a script in R/ (raw files are not committed to Git).
Clean and check with documented, scripted quality control.
Summarise into a small tidy file in data/processed/.
Assess status, trend, and confidence, recorded in data/lookup/indicator_status.csv.
Render the page with Quarto. The homepage report card updates automatically.

title: Methods
text:
Assigning status, trend, and confidence








Call
How it is assigned




Status
Indicator-specific rule, written on each page


Trend
Direction and size of change over the period, with uncertainty


Confidence
High: consistent, frequent, near-complete coverage. Medium: some gaps or method changes. Low: sparse, one-off, or partial coverage

title: Methods
text:
An epidemiologist’s lens
Several indicators borrow ideas from population health surveillance: comparing before and after an outbreak, separating true change from changes in survey effort, and being clear about what a census can and cannot tell us about cause.

title: Report card
section: How to read this report card
text:
How to read this report card

Status summarises recent condition in plain language. It is my independent judgement from the published data, not an official assessment.
Trend describes direction of change over the period shown. Sea temperature is a context indicator, so it has no “good” or “bad” direction.
Confidence is reported separately so a clear trend in patchy data is not mistaken for a certain one.







This is an independent personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NatureScot, the Scottish Government Marine Directorate, JNCC, RSPB, BTO, or SMRU. For official assessments see Scotland’s Marine Assessment 2020.

title: About
text:
I’m Emma Branch, an epidemiologist and health data analyst (PhD candidate, Population and Public Health, UBC) with about ten years’ experience working with linked population data, R, and GIS.
I built this report card to learn about Scotland’s marine environment and its assessment frameworks, and to show how indicator reporting, spatial analysis, and honest communication of uncertainty transfer from population health to marine biodiversity. I am new to Scottish marine ecology, so I have aimed to describe what the data show without overclaiming.

title: Framework map
text: This table is the spine of the project. Each indicator is mapped to the reporting framework it would feed into. Links are my reading of the published documents and are marked as checked once I have confirmed them against the source text.

title: Framework map
text:
Frameworks in brief

Scottish Biodiversity Strategy to 2045: Scotland’s overarching biodiversity strategy and delivery plan.
Marine (Scotland) Act 2010: marine planning, Nature Conservation MPAs, and seal conservation in Scottish territorial waters.
Natural Environment (Scotland) Act: 
Habitats Regulations: protection of SACs and SPAs (the site network formerly part of Natura 2000).
UK Marine Strategy: Good Environmental Status assessed against 11 descriptors.
OSPAR: the North-East Atlantic regional convention; Quality Status Report 2023.
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework: 23 targets for 2030, including Target 3 (30x30).
